 DSWD-Bicol provides P40-M aid amid rising dengue cases
 Oct 22, 2026
 12:00 PM GMT+8
 FOOD AND WATER PROJECT. Personnel of the Department of Social Welfare and Development – Bicol conduct a pre-workshop project implementation review on Tuesday (Oct. 20, 2026) for the Risk Resiliency Program – Project LAWA at BINHI to assess program implementation and identify areas for improvement ahead of 2027. The activity brought the technical working group together to assess the project’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, identify implementation challenges, and set priorities. (Photo courtesy of DSWD-Bicol)
  LEGAZPI CITY – The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) - Bicol Region has released PHP40.39 million in financial assistance to 4,205 dengue patients and bereaved families across the region's six provinces as of Oct. 19.
The agency provided the assistance through its Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program, covering medical assistance, cash relief, funeral assistance, and food assistance.
The agency distributed aid through 13 Crisis Intervention Section - AICS satellite offices and seven Malasakit Centers to help individuals and families manage expenses related to dengue-related illnesses and deaths.
Camarines Norte recorded the highest number of clients served at 1,742, who received PHP13.67 million in assistance, followed by Albay with 1,017 clients and PHP13.24 million.
Sorsogon served 578 clients with PHP7.35 million in aid, while Camarines Sur assisted 612 clients with PHP4.12 million.
Catanduanes recorded 210 clients who received PHP1.51 million, while Masbate served 45 clients with PHP477,400 in assistance.
Meanwhile, DSWD-Bicol has also begun preparations for the 2027 implementation of Project Local Adaptation to Water Access (LAWA) at Breaking Insufficiency through Nutritious Harvest for the Impoverished (BINHI), in anticipation of El Niño's possible effects in the first quarter of next year.
Claudio Villareal, chief of DSWD-Bicol’s Disaster Response and Management Division, said the program's main priority for 2027 is to sustain its gains and ensure established water facilities and communal gardens continue to benefit communities beyond the initial implementation period.
“It is not enough for us to establish water facilities and communal gardens. More importantly, these facilities must be used, properly maintained, and kept productive even after the program’s initial implementation,” he said in an interview on Wednesday. 
He said the agency also plans to strengthen community organizing, capacity building, and partnerships with local government units (LGUs) and other national agencies, helping communities manage water resources and sustain food production independently.
“Our goal is to ensure that Project LAWA at BINHI continues to make a meaningful difference in the lives of vulnerable communities, particularly by improving their access to water, nutritious food, and climate-resilient livelihood opportunities,” he added. 
The specific targets for 2027 will depend on the implementation plan approved by the DSWD Central Office and the availability of funds. 
“For 2026, Project LAWA at BINHI covered 30 LGUs across the six provinces with 9,000 partner-beneficiaries and an allocated budget of PHP78.3 million. DSWD-Bicol reported achieving 100 percent of its target for partner-beneficiaries served,” he said. 
The program is also expected to help vulnerable communities prepare for the potential effects of El Niño through water-harvesting facilities under LAWA and through community-based food production in communal gardens under BINHI.
“Water shortages not only affect people's daily needs but also agricultural activities, food production, and family livelihoods,” he said. 
Through LAWA, communities are assisted in improving their access to water through water-harvesting facilities, while BINHI supports community-based food production through communal gardens.
DSWD-Bicol also identified the sustainability of established water facilities and communal gardens, continued community participation, and support from partner LGUs as key challenges in implementing the program.
“Communities need to sustain planting activities, organize their members, and identify ways to maintain production even after the program’s initial activities have been completed,” he said. (PNA Connie Calipay)
